newsitem.title: QATAR: FEATURE - Independent-minded Qatar seeks limelight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Independent-minded Qatar seeks limelight.

text.p: Seventeen months after toppling his father, Qatar's emir has a firm grip on all levers of power and is setting out to steer his small energy-rich state into the international limelight, officials and diplomats say.

Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani, host of this week's annual meeting of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), has three key assets -- the world's largest single reservoir of natural gas, the support of the United States and other key Western powers, and a motivated team of forward-looking ministers.
A history of automatic deference to Saudi Arabia, the dominant power in the Arabian peninsula, was considered by some young Qataris as an impediment to their national aspirations.
"He never looked beyond Riyadh," said one Western-educated Qatari who blamed the former emir for the country's insularity.
In June 1995 Sheikh Hamad, eldest son of Emir Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad al-Thani, toppled his father in a bloodless palace coup while Sheikh Khalifa was on holiday in Geneva.
Sheikh Hamad's acts during and after the coup stunned Qatar's partners in the GCC -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.
"Saudis are our elder brother, but their policies do not necessarily form the guideline of our national decisions," said a senior Qatari official.
At last year's GCC summit, Sheikh Hamad led his delegation in a walkout when Riyadh pressed its own candidate as the group's general secretary.

In foreign relations, Qatar under the new emir has restored full ties with Gulf War foe Iraq, befriended radical Shi'ite Iran and, until Benjamin Netanyahu came to power in Israel, moved faster than other Gulf countries to normalise relations with the Jewish state -- initiatives at odds with Saudi policy.
ARMS DEALS WITH WEST
Doha also established special relations with Western powers by giving the Pentagon a weapons depot on its soil, and France and Britain lucrative arms deals and business contracts.
U.S. and French companies now dominate Qatar's oil and gas sector which was once the exclusive domain of British Petroleum Co Plc and Royal Dutch/Shell Group.
Qatar is banking its future prosperity and political profile on North Field -- the world's largest single concentration of natural gas at more than 500 trillion cubic feet (14 trillion cubic metres).

Sheikh Hamad's liberal policies have encouraged foreign companies to invest tens of billions of dollars to develop the field and set up a string of costly liquefied natural gas (LNG) and other hydrocarbon-based projects.
Qatar's initial LNG venture is poised to ship its first cargo to Japan on December 24 and is expected to add $374 million to the exchequer in 1997.

According to a recent International Monetary Fund survey, Qatar's export earnings will more than double to $7 billion by 2000 from around $3 billion now, and soar progressively as new projects go on stream.
Qatar's 120,000 native population already enjoys one of the world's highest per capita incomes -- $22,000 -- mainly from oil sales which in 1995 amounted to $2.5 billion.

On the home front, Sheikh Hamad has made moves towards democracy by encouraging public debate, ending press censorship and abolishing the Ministry of Information. He has broken with the Gulf's male-dominated tradition by appointing a woman as undersecretary at the Education and Culture Ministry.
LOCAL ELECTIONS SCHEDULED

He has also scheduled municipal elections to foster grassroots democracy. Speculation is rife that he may order voting to fill certain seats on a 35-member advisory council and give it more powers to oversee the government.

Such acts would have been unthinkable 18 months ago. But "now that we are on the threshold of a new epoch overlooking the 21st Century we aspire to attain the status befitting us," the emir told the council.

Sheikh Hamad's 20-member cabinet is mostly made up of young, Western-educated ministers whose average age is 36, in sharp contrast to the patriarchal, conservative traditions in a region where the average age of the rulers of the five other oil monarchies is 69. Sheikh Hamad is 46.
"It would be wrong to assume that he has no challenges to face," said a senior diplomat. "The most potentially challenging may come from his own father, who lives in exile (in Europe)."
Until a truce was reached in October, Sheikh Khalifa had vowed to regain power "at any cost". He was alleged to have supported a plot in February which Qatar said it foiled.

Official sources confide on condition of anonymity that the former emir has returned $2 billion of missing state funds claimed by the government in worldwide lawsuits following an out-of-court settlement in October.
A final reconciliation on real issues that might clear the way for him to return as father of the nation without any state powers has yet to be worked out, officials say.
